name: Welsh
about: Welsh is spoken by about 538,000 people in Wales, nearly 18 percent of those aged three and over (2021 Census).
It grew from the Brittonic once spoken across most of Britain, so it's older here than English.
It has official status in Wales (the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011), and road signs speak both languages.
It's spoken in Patagonia too: Welsh settlers arrived on the Mimosa in 1865.

lessons.title: Shwmae! Saying hello
intro: Shwmae! I'm Nia. I teach Welsh to anyone who stands still long enough.
Five minutes, a few hellos, and you'll get a smile in every shop from here to Holyhead.

words.note: Friendly and everyday, and understood all over Wales. It began as the southern greeting.
Literally 'how is it?'. Shwmae is the southern squashing-together of the same two words.
dd sounds like the th in 'this'.
For leaving at night, or going to bed.
Hwyl on its own means fun, or the spirit that lifts a crowd.

lessons.tip: Welsh spelling is kind once you know it: w is often a vowel (oo), dd is the th in 'this', and f is a v. Stress usually falls on the last syllable but one.

lessons.title: Diolch! Please, thanks, yes and no
intro: Rhian, pleased to meet you. Dylan Thomas wrote in English, but both his parents spoke Welsh.
Manners first: please, thank you, and the tricky business of saying yes.

words.note: ch as in the Scottish 'loch', never as in 'church'.
What most people actually say to friends.
Welsh has no one word for yes: you echo the verb. Ie is for 'is it this?'.

lessons.tip: Asked 'Wyt ti'n dod?' (are you coming?), you answer with the verb: 'Ydw' (I am) or 'Nac ydw' (I'm not). It's like answering 'Coming?' with 'I am!'.
